title: Concurrency in Java: core concepts
seriesDescription: Threads, synchronized, locks, volatile, executors, CompletableFuture, virtual threads, concurrent collections and classic drills. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: The ideas interviewers probe before any API: shared state, atomicity, visibility, safe publication, deadlock, livelock, starvation, ThreadLocal and Amdahl's law.
source: Java Concurrency in Practice (Goetz et al.); JLS chapter 17 (threads and the memory model); Oracle Java docs (Thread, Object, ThreadLocal, java.util.concurrent); Coffman et al. 1971 (deadlock conditions)

questions.prompt: Two threads run inside the same JVM process. Which of these do they share, while two separate processes would not?

options.text: The heap, including objects and static fields
options.why: Correct: threads of one process live in one address space, so both can reach the same objects. That is why they need synchronization.

options.text: Each other's call stacks and all of their local variables
options.why: Every thread has its own stack; locals are never shared, which is why they are automatically thread-safe.

options.text: Their program counters and saved CPU register state
options.why: Each thread keeps its own program counter and register state so it can be paused and resumed independently.

options.text: Nothing, because the JVM isolates every thread from the rest
options.why: The JVM does not isolate threads. Shared heap access is exactly what makes visibility and race bugs possible.

questions.explanation: A process owns an address space; its threads share the heap and static data but each has a private stack and program counter. Cheap sharing is the benefit of threads and the source of every concurrency bug.

questions.prompt: A data race and a race condition are two names for the same defect.

options.text: True
options.why: Wrong: a data race is unsynchronized conflicting access to one variable; a race condition is a timing-dependent wrong result.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: a program can have a race condition with no data race (two atomic or locked steps in the wrong combination) and a data race that happens to be harmless.

questions.explanation: Check-then-act on a `ConcurrentHashMap` (`containsKey` then `put`) has no data race, yet it is a race condition because another thread can slip in between the two calls. Name which one you mean in an interview.

questions.prompt: Match each symptom to the concurrency property that is violated.

left.text: Two threads run `count++` and one increment disappears
A worker loops forever because it never sees `running = false` written by `main`
A reader obtains a shared object whose fields still hold default values
Two threads wait for each other's locks and neither continues

questions.explanation: The three safety properties are atomicity (compound actions are indivisible), visibility (writes become seen) and ordering (the order observed matches what the code promises). Deadlock is a liveness failure: something good never happens.

questions.text: Deadlock needs four conditions at once: mutual exclusion, {1}, no preemption and circular wait. Taking locks in one global order removes the {2} condition.
questions.explanation: These are the Coffman conditions. Break any one and deadlock cannot occur: one fixed lock order kills circular wait, acquiring everything up front kills hold and wait, and `tryLock` with a timeout lets a thread give a lock back.

questions.prompt: A thread calls `lock.wait()` without having entered `synchronized (lock)`. What happens?

options.text: It throws `IllegalMonitorStateException`
options.why: Correct: `wait()` and `notify()` require the caller to own that object's monitor, and the JVM enforces it at runtime.

options.text: It waits normally and wakes up when another thread notifies it
options.why: There is no lenient mode; the ownership check is mandatory and the call fails before waiting.

options.text: It blocks first until it can acquire the object's monitor
options.why: Waiting for a monitor is what a `synchronized` entry does, not what `wait()` does.

options.text: It fails to compile because the synchronized block is missing
options.why: The compiler cannot see monitor ownership, so this is a runtime error and not a compile error.

questions.explanation: `wait()` must release the monitor it holds while the thread sleeps, so owning it first is a precondition. The same rule applies to `notify()` and `notifyAll()`.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: A daemon thread is a poor choice for a task that must finish writing a file.
questions.reason: The JVM exits once the last non-daemon thread ends, without waiting for daemon threads to complete.

whys.a: Correct: both statements are true, and the reason is exactly why the write may be cut short mid-way.
whys.b: Both are true, but R does explain A, so this option is wrong.
whys.c: R is true, so this option is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so this option is wrong.

questions.explanation: Daemon threads suit background housekeeping such as metrics flushers. Work that must complete should run on non-daemon threads or be awaited with `join` or an executor shutdown.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: An immutable object can be shared between threads without any locking.

whys.a: R does not explain why immutability makes sharing safe, so this option is wrong.
whys.b: Correct: both are true, but R is only one example of an immutable class; the reason is that state which never changes cannot be raced.
whys.c: R is true, so this option is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so this option is wrong.

questions.explanation: Immutable means all fields are `final` and the state cannot change after construction, and the object must be published safely. Immutability turns most thread-safety problems into non-problems.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: A thread can suffer starvation even though no deadlock exists in the program.
questions.reason: Starvation occurs only when threads are deadlocked.

whys.a: R is false, so this option cannot be right.
whys.b: R is false, so option b (both true) is wrong.
whys.c: Correct: A is true (a low-priority or unlucky thread can be denied the lock or CPU indefinitely) and R is false, because starvation needs no cycle of waiting.
whys.d: A is true, so this option is wrong.

questions.explanation: Unfair locks, thread priorities and a greedy thread that keeps re-acquiring a lock can starve others. `ReentrantLock(true)` is a fair lock that grants the lock in arrival order, at some throughput cost.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: Calling `Thread.yield()` guarantees that another runnable thread runs before the caller continues.
questions.reason: `yield()` is only a hint that the current thread is willing to give up the processor.

whys.a: A is false, so this option cannot be right.
whys.b: A is false, so option b (both true) is wrong.
whys.c: A is false, so option c is wrong.
whys.d: Correct: A is false because the scheduler may ignore the hint, and R is true and is exactly why no guarantee exists.

questions.explanation: Never build correctness on `yield()`, `sleep()` timing or priorities. Use proper coordination such as locks, latches or queues.

questions.prompt: A web app stores the current user in a `ThreadLocal` and never calls `remove()`. Requests run on a pooled thread. What is the classic bug?

options.text: A later request on that thread can read the old user's value
options.why: Correct: pool threads outlive requests, so the entry stays attached to the thread and leaks into unrelated work. Clear it in a `finally` block.

options.text: The value is copied into every other thread in the pool
options.why: `ThreadLocal` values are per thread and are not broadcast to other threads.

options.text: The value is garbage collected after each request
options.why: The thread keeps a reference to its entries for as long as it lives, so they are not collected on their own.

options.text: The JVM rejects the second `set()` call
options.why: Calling `set()` repeatedly is fine; it simply overwrites the value for the current thread.

questions.explanation: Besides stale data it can also leak memory when the value holds a big object or a class loader. Always remove the value in `finally`; it is also why `ThreadLocal` and virtual threads need care.

questions.prompt: When is a `ReentrantReadWriteLock` a poor replacement for a plain lock?

options.text: When writes are frequent or the guarded work is tiny
options.why: Correct: the extra bookkeeping then costs more than concurrent readers save, and writers can be starved or block all readers.

options.text: When many threads only read the data and writes are rare
options.why: This is the case it was designed for: readers proceed in parallel and only a writer needs exclusivity.

options.text: When a single reader needs to read the same data twice
options.why: Re-reading is no problem; the read lock can be held across both reads.

options.text: When threads call it from several different classes
options.why: The location of the callers is irrelevant; only the read/write mix and critical-section length matter.

questions.explanation: Measure before switching. For read-mostly data with very short reads, `StampedLock` optimistic reads or an immutable snapshot swapped through a `volatile` reference may beat both.

questions.prompt: Which of these safely publish an object to other threads without any extra synchronization by the readers? Select all that apply.

options.text: Initialize it in a static initializer
options.why: Correct: the JVM's class-initialization lock gives a happens-before edge to every user of the class.

options.text: Store it in a `volatile` field
options.why: Correct: the volatile write happens-before every later read of that field, so the object's state is visible.

options.text: Store it in an ordinary field and read it later
options.why: Without a lock or volatile, the reader may see the reference but stale or default field values.

options.text: Hand it over through a `BlockingQueue`
options.why: Correct: putting an item into a concurrent queue happens-before the matching take on another thread.

options.text: Rely on the object being created before the thread starts reading
options.why: Creation order in wall-clock time creates no happens-before edge, so this guarantees nothing.

questions.explanation: Safe publication means publishing the reference and the object state together via a happens-before edge: a static initializer, a `volatile` or `AtomicReference`, a lock-guarded field, a `final` field of a properly constructed object, or a concurrent collection.

questions.prompt: Two threads each take a lock, fail to get the second, release the first and retry at the same instant, forever. Both stay RUNNABLE. What is this called?

options.text: Livelock, both keep reacting but never progress
options.why: Correct: the threads keep reacting to each other and consuming CPU, yet neither makes progress.

options.text: Deadlock, where both threads sit blocked and idle
options.why: In a deadlock the threads are blocked and idle; here they are actively running.

options.text: Starvation, where one thread is denied
options.why: Starvation means one thread is denied a resource; here both give way to each other in lockstep.

options.text: Priority inversion, a low thread holding a lock
options.why: That involves a low-priority thread holding a lock a high-priority one needs, which is not described here.

questions.explanation: The cure is randomized back-off or a fixed lock order. This is the failure that `tryLock` retry loops can fall into without jitter.

questions.prompt: A job spends 20% of its time in code that cannot run in parallel. By Amdahl's law, what is the maximum possible speedup with an unlimited number of threads?
questions.explanation: Speedup is at most 1 / serial fraction = 1 / 0.2 = 5, no matter how many threads you add. Reducing the serial part (shorter critical sections, less contention) matters more than adding cores.

questions.prompt: A thread enters `synchronized (this)`, calls another `synchronized` instance method on the same object, which calls a third one. How many monitor exits are needed before a second thread can acquire that monitor?
questions.explanation: Monitors are reentrant and keep a hold count: three entries means three exits, and only when the count reaches 0 is the monitor free. `ReentrantLock` behaves the same way with `getHoldCount()`.

questions.prompt: `SimpleDateFormat` is not thread-safe. Write a field declaration that gives each thread its own `SimpleDateFormat` for the pattern `yyyy-MM-dd`.

checks.label: creates the formatter with the pattern

questions.model:
private static final ThreadLocal<SimpleDateFormat> FMT =
    ThreadLocal.withInitial(() -> new SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd"));
questions.explanation: Each thread lazily gets its own copy, so no locking is needed. Other correct solutions exist, for example overriding `initialValue()`. Better still, use the immutable thread-safe `DateTimeFormatter`.

questions.prompt: Inside `catch (InterruptedException e)` of a `Runnable` that cannot rethrow, write the single statement that restores the thread's interrupt status.

checks.label: gets the current thread and calls interrupt()

questions.explanation: Throwing `InterruptedException` clears the interrupt flag. Swallowing it hides the cancellation request from callers up the stack; re-setting the flag lets them notice and stop.

questions.prompt: Thread `main` starts thread `t`, which writes a plain non-volatile field `result`. Then `main` calls `t.join()` and reads `result`. Is the write guaranteed to be visible?

options.text: Yes, because everything `t` did happens-before `join()` returning
options.why: Correct: the Java Memory Model gives a happens-before edge from a thread's last action to a successful `join()` on it.

options.text: No, because the field is not declared volatile or final
options.why: `volatile` is only one way to build an edge; `join()` provides another, so the field needs no extra modifier.

options.text: Only if `t` also used a `synchronized` block before writing
options.why: The write is covered by the `join()` edge regardless of whether `t` used any lock.

options.text: Only if `main` sleeps for a short moment after `join()` returns
options.why: Sleeping does not create happens-before and is never needed after `join()` returns.

questions.explanation: Edges worth remembering: `Thread.start()`, `join()`, monitor unlock/lock, volatile write/read, executor `submit`, `Future.get()` and concurrent-collection hand-offs.

questions.prompt: The Java Language Specification allows a write to a non-volatile `long` to be performed as two separate 32-bit writes, so another thread could see half of it.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: JLS 17.7 permits non-atomic treatment of non-volatile `long` and `double`, so a racy reader may see a torn value.

options.text: False
options.why: Wrong: atomic 64-bit writes are guaranteed only for `volatile` fields, even though most 64-bit JVMs do it anyway.

questions.explanation: Declare shared `long` and `double` fields `volatile` (or use `AtomicLong`) when they are read without a lock. Do not rely on today's JVM behaviour.
